section_summary: This section traces worsening labor conditions in Japan from 1930 through mid-1932, including mass unemployment, falling wages and working hours, strikes, union organization, relief proposals, and labor legislation. It contains a substantial study of Korean immigration and anti-Korean discrimination, followed by an extensive Embassy report on industrial laborers’ earnings, living costs, unions, disputes, and political activity. The final documents describe the merger of Japan’s two principal proletarian parties into the Shakai Taishuto (Socialist Peoples’ Party) and reproduce its platform.

subfiles.title: File note on General Motors dismissals at Osaka
subfiles.about: Records a report concerning the dismissal of 250 General Motors workers and an attempted Embassy mediation.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies a report on labor conditions created by the December 23, 1929 dismissal of approximately 250 workers from General Motors, Japan, Ltd., at Osaka. It highlights Ikuo Oyama’s January 15 request that the American Embassy mediate the dispute.

subfiles.title: Report on the General Motors labor dispute at Osaka
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle, Jr., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes worker protests following General Motors’ dismissal of about 250 Osaka employees and Ikuo Oyama’s appeal for Embassy mediation.
subfiles.summary: General Motors dismissed roughly one-fifth of its Osaka workforce because of declining automobile demand, prompting complaints about the timing and the allowance of only fourteen days’ pay. Workers organized demonstrations, appealed to American unions, and circulated inflammatory handbills. Ikuo Oyama visited the Embassy with supporters, but the chargé declined mediation because the company was incorporated under Japanese law and suspected that Oyama chiefly sought election publicity.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese unemployment during March 1930
subfiles.about: Indexes a report estimating more than 300,000 unemployed people in Japan, including about 65,000 educated unemployed.
subfiles.summary: The file note records the reported extent of unemployment during March 1930. It emphasizes the substantial category of educated unemployed within the official total.

subfiles.title: Monthly Report No. 42 excerpt on unemployment
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle, Jr., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews official and press estimates of unemployment and proposals for government relief during March 1930.
subfiles.summary: Official statistics placed unemployment slightly above 300,000, including about 65,000 educated unemployed, although the Tokyo Jiji reportedly estimated a much larger total. Industrial retrenchment, new graduates, and completion of reconstruction work intensified the problem. The government planned an investigative commission, while proposed remedies included public engineering works, loans to local governments, and reduced military spending.

subfiles.title: File note on Kanegafuchi, Tokyo, and Kobe labor disputes
subfiles.about: Indexes a labor report covering disputes at Kanegafuchi mills and transport strikes in Tokyo and Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Report No. 43 on recent Japanese labor conditions. It lists the Kanegafuchi spinning dispute and strikes by streetcar and bus employees in Tokyo and Kobe.

subfiles.title: Monthly Report No. 43 excerpt on Kanegafuchi Spinning
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains the Kanegafuchi Spinning Company strike over reductions in long-standing wage bonuses.
subfiles.summary: Kanegafuchi Spinning reduced customary bonuses after citing night-work regulation, tariffs, weak trade, falling prices, and the depression. Although most employees belonged to no union, proletarian parties and labor organizations mobilized against the reduction, and about 40,000 workers reportedly became idle. A tentative settlement at the Hyogo mill retained the cut while granting concessions such as cheaper meals.

subfiles.title: Index note for Despatch No. 139 on Korean laborers
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch about Korean immigration, Japanese employee opposition, and discrimination against Korean laborers.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Despatch No. 139 and its detailed report on Korean labor migration into Japan. It foregrounds opposition from Japanese employees and discriminatory treatment of Korean workers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 139 transmitting “Korean Immigration into Japan”
subfiles.about: Transmits an Embassy staff report on Korean immigration into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Castle submits the enclosed study “Korean Immigration into Japan,” prepared by a member of his staff. The covering despatch contains no substantive analysis beyond identifying the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Korean Immigration into Japan
subfiles.from: Member of the American Embassy staff
subfiles.to: Department of State via W. R. Castle, Jr.
subfiles.about: Surveys Korean migration to Japan, its economic causes, geographic distribution, and the discrimination encountered by Korean laborers.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Korean movement to Japan from ancient cultural exchange through industrial migration during and after the First World War, noting the post-earthquake massacre and later restrictions. Statistical tables document entries, departures, and the concentration of Korean residents in major industrial prefectures and cities. It describes Korean immigrants as predominantly unskilled laborers facing unemployment, lower wages, segregation, public hostility, and labor-union demands for exclusion. The report concludes that many Japanese commentators preferred economic development within Korea to formal restrictions on movement within the Empire.

subfiles.title: File note on continuing Kanegafuchi labor troubles
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that the Kanegafuchi Spinning Company dispute was nearing resolution at the end of May.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Report No. 44 on labor trouble during May 1930. It states that negotiations at Kanegafuchi appeared to be approaching a solution.

subfiles.title: Monthly Report No. 44 excerpt on Kanegafuchi negotiations
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports negotiations between Kanegafuchi management and workers during May 1930.
subfiles.summary: Company and worker representatives met during May in an effort to end disputes at the various Kanegafuchi mills. The purported April settlement at the Hyogo mill had not held because workers claimed that management failed to honor its terms, although no major incidents occurred during May.

subfiles.title: File note on unemployed city workers returning to farms
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on the growing rural burden created by unemployed urban workers returning to agriculture.
subfiles.summary: The note records concern that city unemployment was worsening economic conditions in rural areas. It introduces figures showing substantial movement of dismissed factory workers back to the land.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on urban unemployed returning to the countryside
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Quantifies the movement of discharged factory workers back to agricultural communities.
subfiles.summary: Rural economic difficulties were reportedly increasing because large numbers of unemployed city workers were returning to the countryside, even though few prefectures lacked farm labor. Of 41,422 workers discharged in April by larger factories, 17,245 had returned to the land, a marked increase over the preceding year.

subfiles.title: File note and report excerpt on Japanese unemployment
subfiles.about: Reports a rise in official unemployment to 378,500 and continued discussion of relief measures.
subfiles.summary: The Social Bureau of the Department of Home Affairs placed unemployment at 378,500, about 75,000 more than in March. The report stresses that this figure was considered serious in Japan despite appearing modest by United States standards, while relief policies remained unsettled.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 93: Labor in Japan
subfiles.about: Surveys changing employer-worker relations, unionism, labor legislation, education, and selected strikes in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Garrels argues that industrialization was displacing Japan’s paternalistic labor system and fostering class consciousness, unions, and strikes. He describes proposed legal recognition and regulation of unions, expanded workers’ compensation, and educational programs for laborers. The despatch also reports an Osaka eight-hour-day agreement, a major Tokyo textile strike, women’s protests against wage cuts, and government workers’ resolutions against lower wages and dismissals.

subfiles.title: File note on shipyard unemployment and the Fujii Cotton strike
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on shipbuilding layoffs and an unusual chimney protest during a cotton-mill strike.
subfiles.summary: The note highlights severe unemployment in the shipbuilding industry. It also calls attention to an incident at the Fujii Cotton Spinning Company in Kawasaki.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on Mitsubishi layoffs and the chimney-sitter strike
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes Mitsubishi shipyard dismissals, unemployment-relief finance, and a worker’s prolonged chimney protest.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi announced the dismissal of 2,500 shipyard workers at Kobe and Nagasaki, with additional layoffs at Hikoshima, citing the shipbuilding slump, naval limitations, and the depression. The Home Affairs Ministry proposed a ¥50 million public-works loan for unemployment relief. At the Fujii Cotton Spinning Company near Yokohama, a worker remained atop a 180-foot chimney for 130 hours until the strike was settled, prompting legal controversy over the police refusal to supply him with food and water.

subfiles.title: File note on employment prospects for university graduates
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that university graduates would have unusual difficulty finding positions.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies unemployment among the forthcoming class of university graduates as a serious problem. It introduces a report contrasting general scarcity of positions with employers’ interest in prominent athletes.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on graduate unemployment and Miyatake
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports bleak employment prospects for approximately 42,000 graduating students, except for celebrated athletes.
subfiles.summary: About 42,000 college students graduating in the spring were expected to encounter the worst employment market yet. Star athletes remained exceptions: Miyatake, Keio’s noted pitcher, reportedly accepted a post with the Nipponophone Company, strengthening its baseball team.

subfiles.title: File note on the rise in labor disputes
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on a record number of labor disputes and their increasingly violent character.
subfiles.summary: The note records an increase in both the number and severity of Japanese labor controversies. It directs attention to an attached report based on Home Office investigations.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on labor disputes during 1930
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes official findings on the causes and changing occupational scope of labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: Home Office investigations found a record number of settled disputes, about thirty percent more than in the preceding year, although fewer people were involved. Dismissals, reduced or unpaid wages, and lost allowances were principal causes, while disputes spread into occupations such as cinema interpretation, studio work, cafés, acting, dancing, and retail employment.

subfiles.title: File note on acute unemployment and white-collar work
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on deepening unemployment and increased demand for white-collar jobs.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies unemployment as an increasingly acute problem. It particularly emphasizes demand for salaried and white-collar employment.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on Tokyo employment bureaus
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the small proportion of applicants placed by Tokyo employment bureaus and the occupational preferences of educated job seekers.
subfiles.summary: Of 20,437 people applying to the Tokyo Municipal Employment Bureau during May, only 890 found positions through it. Employers increasingly demanded educational qualifications from women, while many educated unemployed resisted manual or lower-status employment in order to preserve white-collar respectability. The specialized bureau for the intelligentsia nevertheless placed about one-third of its applicants.

subfiles.title: File note on unemployment exceeding 400,000
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that Japanese unemployment continued to worsen despite government relief efforts.
subfiles.summary: The note characterizes unemployment as steadily becoming more acute. It refers to newly released Social Bureau figures.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on unemployment in April and May 1931
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Gives national unemployment totals and notes sharp regional increases linked to naval-worker dismissals.
subfiles.summary: Official unemployment rose from 394,625 in April to 401,415 in May, exceeding 400,000 for the first time since official investigations began. Particularly marked increases were reported in prefectures affected by dismissals of naval workers following enforcement of the London Naval Treaty.

subfiles.title: File note for Despatch No. 379, “Japan’s Unemployed”
subfiles.about: Indexes record official unemployment figures for July 1931.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Despatch No. 379 and the Social Bureau’s July unemployment figures. It states that the total was the highest recorded since official investigations began in 1929.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on July 1931 unemployment
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Classifies the 406,923 people officially unemployed in July and gives totals for major prefectures.
subfiles.summary: The Social Bureau reported 406,923 unemployed people in July, an increase of 15,546 over the preceding month and the highest total since investigations began. The report divides them into salaried employees, casual laborers, and other workers, and identifies 168,310 as seeking official relief. Tokyo had by far the largest prefectural total.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum summarizing Salisbury’s labor report
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the principal findings of Salisbury’s study of Japanese industrial laborers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights falling aggregate wages, large wage arrears, unemployment near half a million, reduced working hours, and a cost of living that was beginning to rise after suspension of the gold standard. It also notes low union participation, weak proletarian electoral support, and increasingly numerous and violent disputes. Most disputes were defensive attempts to preserve jobs, wages, and existing conditions rather than campaigns for improvements.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 526 transmitting a report on labor in Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a report on Japanese labor conditions and social unrest as a supplement to an earlier agricultural report.
subfiles.summary: Forbes sends the enclosed report on labor and social unrest in Japan. He explains that it supplements Despatch No. 473 on agricultural conditions.

subfiles.title: Labor in Japan
subfiles.to: Department of State via W. Cameron Forbes
subfiles.about: Analyzes the earnings, living conditions, organization, disputes, political activity, and discontent of Japan’s industrial workforce.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates approximately 4.72 million nonagricultural laborers and documents steep reductions in wages, bonuses, allowances, employment, and working hours between 1928 and 1931. Although many prices had declined, the fall in workers’ actual income was severe, while the yen’s departure from gold was already producing renewed price increases. Union membership remained below eight percent, but the number of unions and labor disputes grew; most disputes sought to resist dismissals, wage cuts, or arrears rather than win new advantages. Proletarian parties performed poorly at elections, yet official and semi-official sources warned of spreading communist influence, violence, and more politically conscious labor activism.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Wage index comparisons, 1928–1930
subfiles.about: Compares wage indexes by industry and sex from 1928 through 1930 using 1926 as the base year.
subfiles.summary: The table shows wage declines across nearly every listed occupation and industry. Textile work and shipbuilding experienced especially large decreases, while the female general index declined more sharply than the male index.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Labor unions by kind of work
subfiles.about: Breaks down Japanese labor unions and their membership by occupational sector.
subfiles.summary: The table lists 712 unions with 354,312 members. Transport and traffic workers accounted for the largest share of membership, followed by metalworkers, while women represented only a small minority of organized workers.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4: Labor-dispute demands in 1930 and 1931
subfiles.about: Compares the demands raised in Japanese labor disputes during 1930 and the first eleven months of 1931.
subfiles.summary: The table records disputes concerning wage increases, wage reductions, calculation systems, working hours, holidays, union freedom, welfare, retirement allowances, and foremen. Objections to reduced wages and demands for discharge or retirement allowances were among the largest specified categories.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 5: Political affiliations of leading labor unions
subfiles.about: Lists major labor bodies supporting the Zenkoku Rono Taishuto and the Shakai Minshuto.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure identifies unions aligned with the National Labor-Farmer Party and gives a combined claimed membership of about 80,000. It separately lists bodies supporting the Social Democratic Party, including seamen, naval workers, shipbuilders, government factory workers, and harbor workers, with a reported total of 224,053.

subfiles.title: File note and excerpt on unemployment during March 1932
subfiles.about: Records continued growth in unemployment despite Seiyukai election promises.
subfiles.summary: The document indexes Despatch No. 560 and states that unemployment continued to increase during March. It notes labor dissatisfaction with government relief policies and refers to Despatch No. 526 for fuller treatment.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Socialist Peoples’ Party
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Despatch No. 72 on the merger of Japan’s two national proletarian parties.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports the creation of the Socialist Peoples’ Party, probably with fewer than 150,000 paying members. It judges such mergers historically insignificant and attributes some membership loss to defections into fascist groups.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 72: Fusion of the Shakai Minshuto and Zenkoku Rono Taishuto
subfiles.about: Reports the formation, leadership, manifesto, and program of the Shakai Taishuto.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the Shakai Minshuto and Zenkoku Rono Taishuto merged on July 24 into the Shakai Taishuto, or Socialist Peoples’ Party, to overcome factional weakness and losses to nationalist-fascist groups. Although the party claimed 300,000 members, the Embassy estimated fewer than 150,000 subscribers. The despatch names the party’s officers and reproduces a manifesto calling for the overthrow of capitalism and resistance to both the extreme left and fascist reaction. Its platform advocates nationalization, labor rights, social insurance, unemployment relief, land reform, progressive taxation, expanded public services, racial equality, disarmament, and protections for workers and tenant farmers.
